levels.title: Present Simple
levels.description: Learn how to use the present simple correctly with he, she and it.

questions.explanation: With he, she and it, add -s to the verb.
With he, use plays, not play.

questions.text: My sister works in a hospital.
questions.correctAnswer: My sister works in a hospital.
questions.explanation: My sister is third-person singular, so work becomes works.
With Tom (he), watch becomes watches.
The bus is singular, so arrive becomes arrives.

questions.text: Anna and Leo walks to school.
questions.correctAnswer: Anna and Leo walk to school.
questions.correction: Anna and Leo walk to school.
questions.explanation: A plural subject takes the base verb: walk.

questions.prompt: Hit the sentence with a mistake.
questions.explanation: Use doesn't with he, she and it.

questions.prompt: Hit the sentence with a mistake.
questions.explanation: After doesn't, use the base form of the verb.

questions.prompt: Hit the sentence with a mistake.
questions.explanation: After doesn't, use like, not likes.

questions.prompt: Hit the sentence with a mistake.
questions.explanation: Study changes to studies with he, she and it.

questions.prompt: Hit the sentence with a mistake.
questions.explanation: After does, use the base verb give.

questions.prompt: Hit the sentence with a mistake.
questions.explanation: The singular subject shop takes closes.
With she, add -s to the verb.

questions.correction: My mother goes to work at 8:00.
questions.explanation: Go becomes goes with he, she and it.
With it, add -s to rain.
Use doesn't + base verb with he, she and it.

questions.text: The baby ___ when it is hungry.
questions.correction: The baby cries when it is hungry.
questions.explanation: A consonant + y changes to -ies for a singular subject.
Use does + subject + base verb in present-simple questions.

levels.title: Past Simple
levels.grammarTopic: Past Simple: regular and irregular verbs
levels.description: Talk about finished actions and choose the correct past form.

questions.correction: We watched a film last night.
questions.explanation: Regular verbs usually add -ed in the past simple.

questions.correction: Maya went to the market yesterday.
questions.explanation: Went is the irregular past form of go.

questions.correction: I lost my keys this morning.
questions.explanation: Lost is the irregular past form of lose.
Play becomes played for a finished past action.
Began is the past-simple form of begin.

questions.text: Sam ___ an email to his teacher.
questions.correction: Sam sent an email to his teacher.
questions.explanation: Sent is the irregular past form of send.

questions.prompt: Hit the sentence with a mistake.
questions.explanation: After didn't, use the base form call.

questions.prompt: Hit the sentence with a mistake.
questions.explanation: After did, use the base form go.

questions.prompt: Hit the sentence with a mistake.
questions.explanation: Didn't is followed by the base form see.

questions.prompt: Hit the sentence with a mistake.
questions.explanation: Did + subject + base verb forms a past question.

questions.prompt: Hit the sentence with a mistake.
questions.explanation: Use understand, not understood, after didn't.

questions.prompt: Hit the sentence with a mistake.
questions.explanation: Bring stays in its base form after did.

options: They did bought a new car.
questions.explanation: Bought is the past form of buy.

questions.correction: Where did you stay last summer?
questions.explanation: Use did to ask about a finished past action.

questions.text: He was tired, so he slept early.
questions.correctAnswer: He was tired, so he slept early.
questions.explanation: Slept is the correct irregular past form of sleep.
Use didn't + base verb.

questions.text: The children ___ very quiet during the test.
questions.correction: The children were very quiet during the test.
questions.explanation: Use were with a plural subject.
After did, use eat, not ate.

levels.title: Present Perfect
levels.grammarTopic: Present Perfect: experiences and recent results
levels.description: Distinguish life experience and unfinished time from a finished past event.

questions.explanation: Use has with he, she and it.
Use have with they.

questions.correction: I have read that book twice.
questions.explanation: Read is the past participle of read; its pronunciation changes.
Lost is the past participle of lose.

questions.correction: We have seen this movie before.
questions.explanation: Seen is the past participle of see.
Train is singular, so use has.
Use past simple with a finished time such as yesterday.

options: Have you ever ridden a horse?
Did you ever ridden a horse?
Have you ever rode a horse?
questions.correctAnswer: Have you ever ridden a horse?
questions.correction: Have you ever ridden a horse?
questions.explanation: Use present perfect for life experience with ever.
Use present perfect for a state continuing until now.
Just normally goes between has and the past participle.
Yet commonly appears with a present-perfect negative.

options: She has gone to Rabat in 2024.
She has went to Rabat in 2024.
questions.explanation: A stated, finished year takes the past simple.

questions.text: She has wrote three emails today.
questions.correctAnswer: She has written three emails today.
questions.correction: She has written three emails today.
questions.explanation: Written is the past participle of write.

questions.correction: How long have you studied English?
questions.explanation: Have is followed by a past participle.

options: They have been here for two hours.
They are here since two hours.
They have been here since two hours.
questions.correctAnswer: They have been here for two hours.
questions.correction: They have been here for two hours.
questions.explanation: Use for with a duration and since with a starting point.

questions.text: Did you finish the report yet?
questions.correctAnswer: Have you finished the report yet?
questions.correction: Have you finished the report yet?
questions.explanation: In this exercise, yet signals present perfect for an unfinished time.

questions.correction: He has lived here since March.
questions.explanation: Since introduces the starting point.
Flown is the past participle of fly.

levels.title: Conditionals & Passive
levels.grammarTopic: First and second conditionals, plus the passive voice
levels.description: Handle real and imaginary conditions, then recognise who receives an action.

options: If it rains, we will stay inside.
If it will rain, we stay inside.
If it rained, we will stay inside.
questions.correctAnswer: If it rains, we will stay inside.
questions.correction: If it rains, we will stay inside.
questions.explanation: Use present simple after if and will in the result clause.

questions.text: If you study, you ___ pass the test.
questions.correction: If you study, you will pass the test.
questions.explanation: The first conditional describes a real future possibility.

options: If I had more time, I would travel.
If I have more time, I would travel.
If I would have more time, I traveled.
questions.correctAnswer: If I had more time, I would travel.
questions.correction: If I had more time, I would travel.
questions.explanation: Use past simple after if and would in the imaginary result.

questions.text: She would help if she ___ the answer.
questions.correction: She would help if she knew the answer.
questions.explanation: An imaginary present condition uses the past simple.

questions.text: If they will arrive early, we start without them.
questions.correctAnswer: If they arrive early, we will start without them.
questions.correction: If they arrive early, we will start without them.
questions.explanation: Use present simple after if and will in the future result.

questions.text: If I were you, I would apologise.
questions.correctAnswer: If I were you, I would apologise.
questions.explanation: Were is standard in the phrase If I were you.

questions.prompt: Hit the sentence with a mistake.
questions.text: English is spoken in many countries.
questions.correctAnswer: English is spoken in many countries.
questions.explanation: Present passive uses am/is/are + past participle.

questions.prompt: Hit the sentence with a mistake.
questions.explanation: The passive needs the past participle built.

questions.prompt: Hit the sentence with a mistake.
questions.correctAnswer: The results will be announced tomorrow.
questions.correction: The results will be announced tomorrow.
questions.explanation: Future passive uses will be + past participle.

questions.prompt: Hit the sentence with a mistake.
questions.text: The rooms are cleaned every morning.
questions.correctAnswer: The rooms are cleaned every morning.
questions.explanation: Are cleaned is the correct present passive for a plural subject.

questions.prompt: Hit the sentence with a mistake.
questions.explanation: Present-perfect passive uses been + past participle; stolen is required.

questions.prompt: Hit the sentence with a mistake.
questions.text: The winner was chosen by the judges.
questions.correctAnswer: The winner was chosen by the judges.
questions.explanation: Was chosen is a correct past-passive form.

options: If I knew, I would tell you.
If I would know, I told you.
If I know, I would told you.
questions.correctAnswer: If I knew, I would tell you.
questions.correction: If I knew, I would tell you.
questions.explanation: The second conditional uses past simple + would + base verb.
The passive needs the past participle sent.

questions.text: If the alarm rings, leave the building.
questions.correctAnswer: If the alarm rings, leave the building.
questions.explanation: An imperative can be the result of a real condition.
Passive questions put the auxiliary before the subject.

questions.text: If he ___ now, he will catch the bus.
questions.correction: If he leaves now, he will catch the bus.
questions.explanation: The if-clause of the first conditional uses present simple.

questions.correctAnswer: This problem can be solved easily.
questions.correction: This problem can be solved easily.
questions.explanation: A modal passive uses modal + be + past participle.
